label: Stimulant medication (methylphenidate / amphetamines)
summary: First-line pharmacological treatment for ADHD with the largest symptom-reduction effects. Listed here as an option on the table, not a treatment started — nothing is in the personal record. Its diagnostic relevance is a caution: because stimulants improve attention in people without ADHD too, feeling better on a trial would not confirm the diagnosis.

label: Cognitive behavioural therapy for adult ADHD
summary: Structured skills-based psychotherapy targeting organisation, planning and impulse control in adults with ADHD; meta-analytic effects comparable to well-established child behavioural treatments. An option on the table, not started.

label: Mindfulness-based therapy
summary: Attention-training and acceptance-based practice studied as an adjunct for ADHD, with moderate meta-analytic effects on inattention and hyperactivity/impulsivity. Promising but tentatively evidenced; an option on the table, not started.

label: Physical exercise (aerobic / cardio)
summary: Regular aerobic exercise as an evidence-based adjunct for ADHD: meta-analyses show moderate improvements in core symptoms and executive function, acutely and chronically, plausibly via catecholamine upregulation in the same direction as stimulants. Modest and dose-dependent (longer/more consistent helps more), a low-risk complement rather than a replacement. An option on the table, not a tracked protocol.

label: Dietary modification (elimination diet, omega-3, additive avoidance)
summary: Dietary approaches to ADHD with modest, variable evidence: restriction/elimination diets help some children (g≈0.29), omega-3 supplementation is modestly effective (below medication), and synthetic-food-color avoidance shows small, bias-prone effects. Not a primary treatment; a low-risk adjunct worth trying with modest expectations for a subgroup. Notably, the sugar-causes-hyperactivity belief is not supported.

label: Sleep management (sleep hygiene, behavioural intervention, melatonin)
summary: Improving sleep as a lever on ADHD: sleep hygiene and brief behavioural sleep strategies are guideline first-line for sleep problems and can reduce ADHD symptoms as well as improve sleep; melatonin reliably advances a delayed sleep phase but does not itself treat ADHD symptoms. A low-risk, high-value adjunct given sleep's role in the differential. An option on the table, not a tracked protocol.
